title: Mind and will (ST I.82)
hook: the mind knows the good and the will loves it
tomorrow: Not money, fame, pleasure or power

segments.voice: Yesterday, the soul and body: for Thomas, the soul is the form of the body, so a person is one living thing. Your line was you are one. What plain kindness did you give your body? Day one thousand one hundred sixty-five.

Which is harder: knowing what's good, or wanting it? A recipe card can tell you exactly how to make soup for a sick friend. It can't make you get up off the couch and chop the onions. A friend can explain, clearly and correctly, why you should call your brother. You can agree with every word and still not dial. Somewhere between seeing a good and going after it, there's a gap. Thomas Aquinas names the two powers on either side of that gap. One sees. One reaches. Today: mind and will.
screen: `KNOWING VERSUS WANTING.` → `THE RECIPE CAN'T CHOP ONIONS.` → `ONE SEES. ONE REACHES.`

segments.voice: Thomas calls them the intellect and the will. The intellect knows: it grasps what things are, and sees what's good. The will is the soul's power to love and choose: it reaches for the good the mind shows it. They work together like this. The mind holds up a good. The will moves toward it. And then the will sets the mind to work again, saying, find me the way there. Thomas makes a striking claim about the will. It can't help wanting happiness. That's built in, the way the eye can't help taking in light. But it isn't forced to choose any particular good on the way, this job or that one, this friend or that habit, because none of those is the whole of happiness. That's where freedom lives. Then the question everyone wants settled: which is greater, mind or will? Thomas gives a careful two-part answer. In itself, he says, the intellect is the higher power. But it depends on what it's aimed at. For things beneath us, knowing them is better than loving them. For God, who is above us, loving God is better than knowing about God. A person can know a great deal of theology and love very little. Paul says something close, in the Douay-Rheims: "Knowledge puffeth up; but charity edifieth." That doesn't make knowing useless. The will can only love what the mind has shown it. Jesus says, in John: "And you shall know the truth, and the truth shall make you free." On Thomas's account: know first, but don't stop at knowing.
screen: `THE MIND SEES THE GOOD.` · `THE WILL REACHES FOR IT.` · `IT MUST WANT HAPPINESS, YET IT CHOOSES.` · `TOWARD GOD, LOVING OUTRANKS KNOWING.` · then, large: `KNOWLEDGE PUFFETH UP; BUT CHARITY EDIFIETH.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: choose one good you know. Settle, and breathe. Let your mind do its work first. Bring up one good thing you already know you ought to do, and haven't. Not a big life change. A thank-you note. A bill. A visit. An apology. See it clearly. Notice why it's good, for you or for someone else. Then hand it to the will. Picture yourself actually doing it, step by step, today. Notice where you balk. Don't argue. Just choose it again, quietly. If you pray, you can ask God for the strength to carry it out. The bell holds the time.
Mind and will. The intellect sees the good; the will loves and chooses it. For Thomas, they work as a pair, and toward God, loving outranks knowing. Today's word.
Your line: know, then love. Today, do the one good thing you already know about, before you go looking for more to know. Day one thousand one hundred sixty-five.

howItsDone: Catholic moral teaching, drawing on Thomas, speaks of the intellect and the will as the two spiritual powers of the soul, and examinations of conscience often ask both what a person knew and what they chose.

match.prompt: mind and will — tap the pairs.
pairs: the will can't help wanting it

myth: for Thomas, the will can choose not to want happiness at all
he says the will can't help wanting happiness. it's free in choosing the particular goods along the way.
Thomas says loving God is better than knowing about God
in itself the intellect is higher, but toward God, who is above us, love outranks knowledge.

the mind shows the will a good; the will then sets the mind to work finding the way.

fork.setup: you're Thomas. a student asks: which is greater, the mind or the will? what do you answer?
options: the mind, always and in every case.
the mind in itself, but toward God, loving is better than knowing.
the will, always and in every case.
fork.reveal: Thomas gives a two-part answer: in itself the intellect is higher, but for things above us, like God, love outranks knowledge.

original.note: Latin, the language Thomas wrote in: the intellect and the will.

trapdoor: what you thought: willpower is just trying harder.
what it means: the will is the soul's power to love and choose the good the mind shows it.
what a scholar hears: Thomas says the will wants happiness by necessity but chooses particular goods freely, which is where freedom lives.

notes: All Aquinas is paraphrased. Check: the will desires happiness of necessity (I.82.1) but does not necessarily will particular goods (I.82.2); intellect simply higher than will, yet love of God better than knowledge of God, while knowledge of lower things is better than love of them (I.82.3); intellect moves will as end, will moves intellect as agent (I.82.4).
The eye-and-light comparison is the script's own image, not Thomas's.
Douay-Rheims wording to confirm: 1 Corinthians 8:1 ('Knowledge puffeth up; but charity edifieth'); John 8:32.
Editor: the closing line is now framed as Thomas's account, not the narrator's instruction.
